title: Δρύες καὶ Ζεύς
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 99 (= Perry 302). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Αἱ δρύες κατεμέμφοντο τοῦ Διὸς λέγουσαι ὅτι « μάτην παρήχθημεν ἐν τῷ βίῳ· ὑπὲρ πάντα γὰρ τὰ φυτὰ βιαίως τὴν τομὴν ὑφιστάμεθα. »
sentences.tr: Hai dryes katememphonto tou Dios legousai hoti « matēn parēchthēmen en tōi biōi· hyper panta gar ta phyta biaiōs tēn tomēn hyphistametha. »
sentences.l: The oaks were finding fault with Zeus, saying that « in vain we were brought forth in life; for beyond all the plants we undergo the cutting by violence. »
sentences.i: The oaks reproached Zeus, saying: « We were brought into the world to no purpose; more than any other growing thing we endure a violent felling. »
sentences.n: καταμέμφομαι takes the genitive of the party blamed, τοῦ Διός. The ὅτι before the quotation is the recitative ὅτι: it introduces words quoted directly, and English leaves it untranslated — the guillemets do its work. παρήχθημεν, aorist passive of παράγω, is 'we were brought forward, produced'.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ Ζεύς· « Ὑμεῖς αὐταὶ αἴτιοι τῆς τοιαύτης ἑαυταῖς καθεστήκατε συμφορᾶς· εἰ μὴ γὰρ τοὺς στειλειοὺς ἐγεννᾶτε, καὶ πρὸς τεκτονικὴν καὶ γεωργικὴν χρήσιμοι ἦτε, οὐκ ἂν πέλεκυς ὑμᾶς ἐξέκοπτεν. »
sentences.tr: Kai ho Zeus· « Hymeis autai aitioi tēs toiautēs heautais kathestēkate symphoras· ei mē gar tous steileious egennate, kai pros tektonikēn kai geōrgikēn chrēsimoi ēte, ouk an pelekys hymas exekopten. »
sentences.l: And Zeus: « You yourselves have become the cause to yourselves of such a misfortune; for if you did not bring forth the axe-handles, and were not useful for carpentry and for farming, no axe would be cutting you down. »
sentences.i: And Zeus replied: « You have brought this misfortune on yourselves; for if you did not give birth to the axe-handles, and were not useful for carpentry and for farming, no axe would be cutting you down. »
sentences.n: Καὶ ὁ Ζεύς· has no verb of saying at all — the article and the colon are enough, and the idiomatic line supplies 'replied'. καθεστήκατε is the perfect of καθίστημι used intransitively, 'you have come to stand as, you have become': the oaks did not make themselves the cause, they became it. The whole second half is a present contrary-to-fact condition: imperfect indicative in both limbs with ἄν in the apodosis — 'if you were not (as in fact you are), no axe would be (as in fact it is)'. αἴτιοι is masculine although the oaks are feminine (ὑμεῖς αὐταί, ἑαυταῖς); Chambry prints it so and it is left as printed. στειλειός is the helve, the wooden handle into which the iron head is fitted: the oak supplies the very timber that carries the blade against it.

sentences.t: Αἴτιοί τινες ἑαυτοῖς τῶν κακῶν καταστάντες τὴν μέμψιν ἀφρόνως τιθέασι τῷ θεῷ.
sentences.tr: Aitioi tines heautois tōn kakōn katastantes tēn mempsin aphronōs titheasi tōi theōi.
sentences.l: Certain men, having become the cause to themselves of their troubles, senselessly lay the blame on the god.
sentences.i: Some men bring their troubles on themselves, and then senselessly lay the blame on the god.
sentences.n: καταστάντες is the aorist participle of the same καθίστημι that Zeus used of the oaks (καθεστήκατε): the moral repeats his word back. τίθημι with the dative is 'lay upon'. τῷ θεῷ names no god — 'the god', the divine as such — though it is Zeus the oaks blamed.
